teaching.causalExplanation: Start with a simpler set, where grouping isn't needed. Our twenty sampled students told us how many screens are in their bedroom, from none to three. Count them with a tally, one mark for each answer, crossed off in fives. A tally is quick to fill in as answers arrive, and the fives make counting easy. Three students said none, seven said one, six said two, and four said three. Each count is a frequency, how many times a value occurs. Written in a table, that's a frequency table, and the frequencies add to twenty, one for each student. Here it works well, because there are only four possible values, and lots of students share each one. Now try the same thing with screen time. Seventy minutes, once. Ninety-five, once. A hundred and ten, once. The table is thirty rows of ones, and it tells us nothing. When nearly every value is different, we group the values into classes and count each class instead. Here, classes sixty minutes wide work well. Sixty to under a hundred and twenty, a hundred and twenty to under a hundred and eighty, and so on, up to four hundred and eighty. Remember the survey buttons? A box for every answer, no overlaps, no gaps. Classes follow the same rule. A hundred and twenty sits in a hundred and twenty to under a hundred and eighty, never in two classes at once. Now tally again. Three, nine, seven, five, three, two and one, thirty in all. We lose the exact values, but we gain a picture we can actually read. Why sixty minutes? Watch what happens if we change the width. Classes twenty minutes wide give lots of ones and twos, and the graph looks like a picket fence. Classes two hundred minutes wide squash everything into two big bars and a lone one. Somewhere between, the shape appears. Most students sit between two and four hours, with a few much higher. A good rule is about five to ten classes, all the same width, starting at a tidy value below the smallest number, and covering the largest. That's why some datasets need grouping. Without it, we can't see the shape, and we can't analyse it.

scenes.teachingReason: A histogram is a column graph for numerical data. The horizontal axis is a number line, here screen time in minutes. Each class gets a bar, and its height is the class's frequency, so a bar's height tells you how many students are in that class. Three for sixty to a hundred and twenty. Nine for the next. Then seven, five, three, two and one. Notice the bars touch. That's because the classes meet. One class ends exactly where the next one begins, so there's no gap on the number line, and no gap between the bars. The tallest bar is the class with the most students, a hundred and twenty to under a hundred and eighty minutes. Gaps between bars are for categories, like bedroom and kitchen, which we'll draw soon.

scenes.teachingReason: A frequency polygon draws the same shape as a line. Put a dot in the middle of the top of each bar, at its class centre, halfway between the class's ends. Sixty to a hundred and twenty has its centre at ninety, so the first dot sits at ninety, height three. Then a hundred and fifty, height nine, and so on to four fifty. Join the dots. Then close the polygon on the axis, at the centres of the empty classes on either side, thirty and five hundred and ten. The polygon and the histogram tell the same story. The line just makes it easier to see the rise and the long, slow fall on the right. Some questions show only the polygon, so you need to read it either way.
